post.description:
The body is the rows, in one of three formats, chosen by `Content-Type`: `application/json` (an array of row objects), `application/x-ndjson` (one row object per line) or `application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream` (an Arrow IPC stream, matched to columns by field name).

Values are checked against the table's column types and never coerced. A batch is all or nothing: one bad value rejects it with every problem listed by row and column, and nothing is written. On an upsert table a row whose key exists replaces the old row, and a row equal to the one stored is skipped: it counts as neither written nor replaced, and a batch of such rows changes nothing and is visible at once.

Rows become visible to queries at the next epoch (within `epoch_interval`); `?wait=visible` answers only once they are. An `Idempotency-Key` header makes retries safe: a key seen in the last 24 hours gets the first response again and writes nothing. A `503` means the server is busy; retry after `Retry-After` seconds.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key

put.description: The body is the table's complete new contents, in the same formats as writing: its rows are written (a row whose key exists replaces the old one), and every row whose key isn't among them is deleted, in one batch that becomes visible at once. For keeping a dimension in step with a system of record that can only be read whole (an asset tree, a product catalogue): send all of it every time, and what disappeared there disappears here. Rows that are already as sent are skipped, so sending the same contents again changes nothing. `replaced` counts rows replaced and rows deleted. Only upsert tables have keys, so only they can be replaced.

post.description:
The body is the rows, in one of three formats, chosen by `Content-Type`: `application/json` (an array of row objects), `application/x-ndjson` (one row object per line) or `application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream` (an Arrow IPC stream, matched to columns by field name).

Values are checked against the table's column types and never coerced. A batch is all or nothing: one bad value rejects it with every problem listed by row and column, and nothing is written. On an upsert table a row whose key exists replaces the old row, and a row equal to the one stored is skipped: it counts as neither written nor replaced, and a batch of such rows changes nothing and is visible at once.

Rows become visible to queries at the next epoch (within `epoch_interval`); `?wait=visible` answers only once they are. An `Idempotency-Key` header makes retries safe: a key seen in the last 24 hours gets the first response again and writes nothing. A `503` means the server is busy; retry after `Retry-After` seconds.

parameters.description: `visible`: answer once the rows are visible to queries.

put.description: The body is the table's complete new contents, in the same formats as writing: its rows are written (a row whose key exists replaces the old one), and every row whose key isn't among them is deleted, in one batch that becomes visible at once. For keeping a dimension in step with a system of record that can only be read whole (an asset tree, a product catalogue): send all of it every time, and what disappeared there disappears here. Rows that are already as sent are skipped, so sending the same contents again changes nothing. `replaced` counts rows replaced and rows deleted. Only upsert tables have keys, so only they can be replaced.

post.description: A view is a dashboard that lives only in the server's memory: checked by the same rules as a dashboard file and shown live like one (`open_dashboard` with its id), but never written to the config, versioned or committed. For an answer an agent shows once; saving it as a dashboard is a config change like any other. The body is a dashboard file as JSON (the `dashboard` schema); a visual without `at` is placed for you. A view nobody opens for 24 hours is forgotten, and at most 1000 are kept.

get.description: Upgrades to a WebSocket speaking the live protocol: JSON messages tagged by `type` (`ClientMessage` in, `ServerMessage` out). A session holds a selection with back/forward history and shows one dashboard; the server sends one frame per epoch with whatever changed on it, and answers selection changes right away. Browsers can't set headers on a WebSocket, so the read token may also come as `?token=`.
